Salut, c’est Nantou !\n\nDans cet articl:
Hi, it’s Nantou!

In this article, I wanted to understand how Generation Z sees feminism and makes it its own. Have its members reinvented it, or are they part of the continuity of struggles waged before they were born, the ones that marked the last century, from the right to vote to the sexual revolution, from the legalization of abortion to the fight for pay equity?
Plutôt que de raconter simplement un ver: Rather than simply recount an exhibition opening, I wanted to capture an energy: that of a generation that dares to speak about itself, put itself on display and turn its lived experience into art. For many of the artists who took part in the event, it was a first. A first exhibition, a first time speaking publicly. These experiences struck me as precious and important to tell, because they also reveal something about feminism as Generation Z sees it. It is plural, intersectional, shaped by different lived experiences, but driven by the same desire: to open doors so that others, in turn, can walk through.
<strong>Ils sont nés après 1995. On les: They were born after 1995. They are called “Generation Z.” Before they were born, feminist struggles transformed society; think of the right to vote, the sexual revolution of the 1960s, the legalization of abortion or pay equity. But these battles, often led by white, middle-class women, remain siloed. They have rarely taken in the realities of racism, youth, religion or gender identity, and it is precisely this vision that 11 racialized young women and non-binary people of Generation Z want to open up in the collective exhibition Briser les murs.
<strong>Durant 10 mois, ils et elles ont: Over 10 months, they worked to bring out what had until then stayed confined to notebooks, cellphones or conversations between friends. On opening night, their photographic works, videos, installations and performances took their place in a gallery for the first time. “We’re young, we’re racialized, and we don’t take that for granted,” says Rose, one of the exhibiting artists. “It’s a blessing to have this opportunity.”
<strong>Pour celles et ceux qui n’avaien: For those who never imagined seeing their work hung in a gallery, that is already a wall broken through. Intimacy, anger, hope: registers that, for the length of an exhibition, give a voice to young people who are often made invisible in Quebec’s cultural landscape, and who had a platform that night to tell their own stories. We invite you to dive into the heart of this first exhibition, through the eyes of three young artists and of those who came to listen to them.
Il est 18 h. La nuit tombe doucement sur: It is 6 p.m. Night is falling gently on Saint-Laurent Boulevard, but the street isn’t sleeping. The bars are slowly filling up and the nightclubs aren’t open yet, but the notes of a DJ set drift through the window of WIP, an art gallery. This is where these young artists’ first exhibition is being held. The event is sold out, but the doors stay open for those who are pulled in by the music or intrigued by the colourful posters pasted on the façade. “Not too young to be infantilized, not too young to be judged, not too young to face racism, not too young to lead, not too young to be sexualized,” reads one of them. The tone is set: here, feminism is in dialogue with other struggles. And these words find an immediate echo among the audience. Dior, from Generation Z, sticks a sticky note on the wall at the back of the room: “Intersectionality shines.”
« L’intersectionnalité fait briller » :: “Intersectionality shines”: one of the many messages left by visitors on the collective wall. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Pour elle, impossible de parler de fémin: For her, it is impossible to talk about feminism without talking about multiple identities. “I’m a woman, but I’m also a Black woman. The issues aren’t the same. A white woman can demand pay equity; me, I already have to fight just to get hired.” She points out that Generation Z goes “a little further” than previous generations in this thinking. “Our parents, for example, focused on the condition of women in general. We also point out the blind spots, what other struggles don’t take into account.”
<strong>Capter l’invisible, une photo à: Capturing the invisible, one photo at a time
Et ces « angles morts » sont mis en lumi: And these “blind spots” are brought to light in an exhibition of photography, visual art and film. The artists wanted to go beyond feminism alone to speak about other generational realities. “We sat down together, we put on the table what we were living, what had marked us. That’s where our photos came from,” says Rose, 20, who worked on the exhibition.
Ces clichés expriment ce que les mots pe: These images express what words sometimes struggle to say: racism, ageism, or social isolation, that diffuse feeling that runs through her generation. “We tried to make people understand that you can be surrounded, you can have friends, and still keep feeling alone. And that’s what a lot of people live,” she says.
L’une des premières images que le specta: One of the first images visitors encounter as they move through the exhibition shows a woman frozen in a shaft of light, surrounded by blurred silhouettes with their backs turned to her. For Yann, a visitor not very familiar with feminist debates, this photo strikes a deep chord: “I still recognized myself in this photo. Because it’s not a feeling that only has to do with women. Men too, sometimes, we can be surrounded, but we can feel alone too.” While he admits he doesn’t yet have “a firm opinion on feminism,” he adds: “I think we have to respect and value differences.”
Une des photos de l'exposition photo : u: One of the photos in the exhibition: a woman frozen in a shaft of light, surrounded by blurred silhouettes, an image of the social isolation felt by Generation Z. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Un autre cliché, plus frontal, met en sc: Another, more confrontational photo shows a young Black woman in professional attire, seated on a chair. Behind her stands a white man whose face is only half visible and whose hands rest on her shoulders. “We’re tired of not being taken seriously because we’re young. Tired of being told we don’t have the right to speak,” Rose insists. A deliberately unsettling image that evokes racism, sexism and that inner loneliness all at once.
Ce cliché révèle la pression constante q: This photo reveals the constant pressure faced by racialized Generation Z. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Rose dit avoir été transformée par ce pr: Rose says she was transformed by this project. A student in accounting and management, she never imagined that one day her work would hang at WIP. “It’s a grace, a blessing to have been able to show my photos to the public and to be recognized as an artist, even if that wasn’t my primary identity. It’s extraordinary to have been able to live this together, to have this recognition,” she says, moved. “Being a feminist in our generation means fighting for what’s ours, but also defending our culture, our choices, our freedom.” Yet feminism wasn’t a subject in her family, she explains. “In Africa [in Cameroon], it wasn’t a priority. Here, my father sees what I go through, the difficulties, the struggles, and he understands more easily.”
Enfin, elle met en lumière une tension q: Finally, she highlights a tension that, in her view, runs strongly through her generation: “We’re trying to be freer, but we get sexualized much faster.” Between the desire for emancipation and a reductive social gaze, this is, in her eyes, one of the great feminist issues of our time.
<strong>Quand l’écran devient le miroir: When the screen becomes a mirror of wounds
Pour Myriam, 19 ans, « le féminisme, c’e: For Myriam, 19, “feminism is a voice.” A universal, unifying movement that lets people make things change. She found that voice in film.
Dans une petite salle, au fond de la gal: In a small room at the back of the gallery, her short film plays on a loop. It takes the form of an audiovisual collage, with a soundtrack she narrates, and it addresses the theme of violence against women. “I made a short film talking about violence, whether it’s street harassment, sexual assault and everything that comes with that,” explains Myriam, whose work grew out of an intimate experience.
Le court métrage de Myriam, construit co: Myriam’s short film, built as an audiovisual collage, denounces street harassment and violence against women. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
« L’idée des regards sur mon corps me do: “The idea of people’s eyes on my body makes me feel like a piece of meat,” she says. “It’s not because of what I’m wearing, it’s because we live in a society where we’re only seen as objects of gratification.”
Son film ne s’arrête pas aux agressions: Her film doesn’t stop at visible assaults; it also addresses wounds that are less obvious but just as destructive. Gaslighting, manipulation, blame… so many forms of psychological violence that leave their mark. “We talk a lot about physical or sexual abuse, but not enough about mental violence. Yet it destroys too,” she insists. “I wanted to find the courage to talk about this,” she says.
Originaire du Maroc, Myriam se souvient: Originally from Morocco, Myriam remembers experiencing street harassment as early as adolescence, but also more recently in Montréal. “I started seeing people calling out to me in the street, not like ‘insults,’ but with words to try to hit on me in a more perverted way,” she says. For her, this phenomenon crosses borders. “It exists everywhere. You could be a tourist in another country, and every man you walk past will call out to you,” she says.
Avec son film, Myriam veut avant tout mo: With her film, Myriam above all wants to show that this violence must not condemn women to silence or isolation. “I wanted to show that you can always find the courage to speak and ask for help so you don’t feel alone.”
Pour elle, l’image a un pouvoir particul: For her, the image has a particular power. More than words, film allows her to give shape to her experiences and share them. Seeing her short film projected on a big screen, in a full room, turned this intimate experience into public speech.
Dans la salle, le silence règne. Sophie,: In the room, silence reigns. Sophie, an audience member, says as she leaves that she was deeply moved by Myriam’s film. “The images, the words, everything resonates because these are realities that many women know,” she says. For her, the choice of an audiovisual collage strengthens the power of the message: “You can feel that it’s not just a personal story, but something that concerns all of us.”
Myriam souligne que sa démarche est égal: Myriam stresses that her approach is also a quest for solidarity. “I wanted to show that women can connect with each other, not feel alone.” Before Fem-Artz, Myriam didn’t define herself as a feminist, for lack of a role model. The collective gave her a space to experiment, put words to her intuitions and understand that her personal experience could resemble that of other women.
Pour elle, le féminisme, c’est aussi ref: For her, feminism also means rejecting the demands repeatedly placed on women: get married, seek a man’s validation, dress to please. “We don’t need a man to tell us what we should be,” she says flatly.
<strong>Dialogues entre générations : mé: Dialogues between generations: yesterday’s memory, today’s hopes
L’événement bat son plein, la musique co: The event is in full swing, the music keeps making the walls vibrate and, in a corner of the room, Asmaa studies the photos at length. A member of the Canadian Council of Muslim Women, she knows all too well the importance of these collective moments. For her, this exhibition is a reminder that the next generation really does exist. “In our feminist organizations, it’s often older women. We have to encourage young people to take their place. They’re the future,” she says with conviction.
Originaire d’Égypte, elle est arrivée au: Originally from Egypt, she arrived in Canada in the 1960s, just as Western feminism was redefining itself. “It was the beginning of feminism in the United States, we saw women wanting to take their place. And it was also the sexual revolution, the arrival of the pill,” she remembers.
Pour la jeune adulte qu’elle était alors: For the young adult she was then, it was a shock: leaving a country locked down by an authoritarian regime where it was forbidden not only to talk about politics but also about social change, and discovering a society where women could speak out, make demands, study. “I wanted to flourish, to live in a more open society.”
Aujourd’hui, devant les œuvres de Rose,: Today, standing before the works of Rose, Myriam and the others, Asmaa says she sees a passing of the torch. She measures the differences between her era and that of Generation Z. “In my time, there were fewer subtleties. It was women, in contrast with men. Now, young people talk about gender equality, about in-between realities, about non-binary people.” She sees not a rupture but a continuity. Each generation, she says, reinvents its struggles.
Son regard demeure réaliste. Elle sait q: Her outlook remains realistic. She knows that progress can be reversed. She cites the example of the United States, where the right to abortion has been challenged in several states. “Progress is never guaranteed. That’s why we have to keep fighting,” she insists. Yet despite her clear-sightedness, Asmaa says she is full of hope. Seeing these racialized young people exhibit their work for the first time, giving shape to their wounds and their struggles, is for her a promise. “What matters is that the chain doesn’t stop. Every generation has its urgencies, but we must never break the thread.”
Non loin, Morgane, milléniale et travail: Not far away, Morgane, a millennial who works in the field of domestic violence, looks around attentively. For her, it isn’t just an exhibition but a reminder: “The same themes keep coming back, but that’s very significant. It means something.” She cites the body, being made invisible, sisterhood, the difficulty of learning to love yourself and of building yourself under the gaze of others. “These are the same realities, the same battles I had to face and that I continue to face,” she says, her voice steady.
Morgane, une des spectatrices, voit dans: Morgane, one of the audience members, sees in this exhibition a fresh breath for feminism, carried by the next generation. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Elle ne voit pas une rupture radicale en: She doesn’t see a radical break between millennials and members of Generation Z, but rather another way of speaking out: “Maybe the difference is in the way of approaching it, of voicing it. They show it through art, in an exhibition.”
Elle reconnaît qu’elle avait une certain: She admits she had some apprehension before coming: “With all the statistics we hear, I was a bit afraid that Generation Z was going back toward more traditional values. But what I saw here were rich, distinctive approaches. Each of them has her own way of expressing the struggle.”
Ce qui l’a le plus marquée, c’est l’expr: What struck her most was the expression of bodies: the dance performance, but also the physical presence of the artists in the room. “It was well placed, not disjointed. It was about taking up space, being comfortable in your body,” she says. And she concludes, with a smile: “There is a next generation. It’s interesting, and above all reassuring.”
Alexandra, elle aussi milléniale et acti: Alexandra, also a millennial and a seasoned activist, says she is “comforted to see that the next generation is getting involved and that BIPOC voices, rarely heard, can be put on display.”
<strong>Cohabiter, se relier, lutter ens: Living side by side, connecting, fighting together
La soirée bat son plein. Les spectateurs: The evening is in full swing. Visitors move from one photo to the next, stop in front of an installation, resume walking toward a video. The flow is continuous, almost organic. In the middle of this movement, one figure stands out: Ritej, 19, is wandering too, but with particular attention. She stops, exchanges a few words, explains an image to anyone who asks. Sometimes she simply answers a question, casting a knowing look at the work she helped stage.
Ritej, une des artistes, croit que le fé: Ritej, one of the artists, believes feminism is a form of humanism. By taking part in the exhibition’s design, she wanted to show that even when we are different, coexistence is possible. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Avec d’autres, elle a réfléchi à la scén: With others, she thought about the exhibition’s design: how the layout, lighting and colours could extend the message about the nature of feminism for Generation Z. In the gallery, blue and orange lights, two seemingly opposite shades, coexist to create an unexpected harmony. A visual metaphor for what Briser les murs seeks to make people feel: differences that, put together, make up a shared story. “That’s what we wanted people to feel: even if we’re different, we can blend, coexist; and it becomes beautiful.”
Cette quête d’harmonie résonne avec son: This quest for harmony resonates with her own journey. Originally from Montréal-Nord, Ritej says how much this project allowed her to open up. “I met people who don’t look like me, who come from elsewhere. It changed the way I see things,” she says.
Son féminisme, elle le définit comme une: She defines her feminism as a form of humanism: “Everyone deserves to live fully, without discrimination.” She extends the struggle to injustices based on religion, skin colour, sexual orientation, appearance. Ritej wears the hijab and knows the prejudices that come with it. “People often say feminism doesn’t exist for women who wear the veil. But that’s totally false. My veil doesn’t define me. It’s a choice I make for myself, not for men. For me, it fits perfectly with feminism: choosing what you want to do with your body and your life.”
Elle insiste : même si elle ne subit pas: She insists: even if she doesn’t directly experience every form of discrimination, she fights for those who do. “Just as our ancestors fought for us,” she says, convinced that each generation must play its part in the chain of struggles.
« Quand on parle de libération collectiv: “When we talk about collective liberation, each and every one of us has a part to play,” Fem-Artz project and mobilization coordinator Taïna Mueth reminded the audience in the exhibition’s opening speech. That evening, her words found a direct echo in the works and voices of the young exhibitors: to go beyond the walls between struggles, refuse to silo battles and show that the intimate can become a collective force.
